doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: His father's thwarted career, and the Panthers and Black power friends
summary: His father trained in drafting but was kept to menial plant work; Ridley recalls friendships with Rap Brown, Baraka and the Panthers.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Guess what? A man with this kind of knowledge. He went around to the machines and was a chip collector. Putting it in — you know, cleaning up. Because they wouldn’t hire him because of his color. You know that kind of craziness. I mean here’s a man, who knows what he could have contributed if he had been given the opportunity. That’s why I try to tell the young African-American kids now — you don’t realize the dues that people paid. And this whole thing about getting out to vote? Hey, I came up through that thing. You know I was friendly with Rap Brown and Amiri Baraka and all these guys and Stokley Carmichael, all these guys. And people want to put the Panthers down, like Huey Newton and Bobby Seale and all them. Those guys — they started out, the government and other nefarious groups that painted the picture of them being the enemies of the state.
